svg.aria-label: How a Hive table and an Iceberg table each resolve a query, the three AWS owners of Iceberg table maintenance with their default values, and the seven ways maintenance deletes files or stops without raising an error
svg.title: A Hive table on Amazon S3 answers a query by reading its partition list from the AWS Glue Data Catalog and then listing every object under each prefix, which is why the scale figures do not line up: Glue will hold ten million partitions for one table while Athena cannot read more than one million partitions in a single scan, a factor of ten. An Apache Iceberg table answers the same query by following a pointer in the catalog to a metadata file, then to a snapshot, then to a manifest list, then to manifests that carry per-column bounds, so pruning happens before any data file is opened and a commit is a single atomic pointer swap. What that costs is maintenance, and AWS offers three owners for it with different defaults. Running OPTIMIZE and VACUUM in Athena yourself gives a snapshot age of four hundred and thirty two thousand seconds, which is five days, a minimum of one snapshot, one hundred metadata files kept, no rewrite below five data files or two delete files per data file, across Parquet, ORC and Avro. AWS Glue Data Catalog table optimizers run continuously on thresholds, targeting five hundred and twelve megabyte files, triggering above one hundred files, ignoring any file at or above three hundred and eighty four megabytes, deleting at most one million files per run, suspending after four consecutive failures, and supporting Parquet only. Amazon S3 Tables runs maintenance for you with a snapshot age of one hundred and twenty hours, again five days, a minimum of one snapshot, a five hundred and twelve megabyte compaction target configurable between sixty four and five hundred and twelve, a Parquet row group default of one hundred and twenty eight megabytes so a compacted file holds four row groups, up to ten times higher transactions per second, and a quota of ten table buckets per Region. None of the seven listed failures raises an error when it matters: two Glue tables sharing one S3 location, a bucket-wide lifecycle expiration rule over the table path, an Iceberg history expiry property set on an S3 table, a user-defined branch or tag on an S3 table, four consecutive compaction failures, orphan file deletion skipping everything created on or before its own creation date, and VACUUM running without permission to delete objects.

g.text: The file list moved into the table — and now it has to be pruned
Iceberg fixes what schema-on-read could not. What it adds is a maintenance schedule with a five-day default.
1. How a query finds its files
catalog partition list → S3 LIST per prefix → whatever is under it
Glue holds up to 10,000,000 partitions for one table.
Athena reads at most 1,000,000 in a single scan — a factor of ten.
pointer → metadata file → snapshot → manifest list → manifests
Manifests carry per-column bounds, so pruning happens before
a data file is opened. A commit is one atomic pointer swap.
2. Three owners of maintenance, three sets of defaults
You run it, or it does not run
Ignores files at or above — 384 MB
3. None of these raises an error at the time it matters
Two Glue tables sharing one S3 location — one table's optimizer deletes files the other still references.
A bucket-wide lifecycle expiration rule over the table path — deletes files referenced by active snapshots.
history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms set on an S3 table — snapshot management fails for the whole table.
A user-defined branch or tag on an S3 table — same outcome: nothing expires, and metadata keeps growing.
Four consecutive compaction failures — the Glue optimizer suspends itself and still looks enabled.
Orphan file deletion never touches a file created on or before the optimizer's own creation date.
VACUUM without s3:DeleteObject — the query succeeds and not one file is removed.
One table, one prefix, one deleter — and an alarm on whether the maintenance job still runs.
